It details the report’s basis for preparation, sustainability governance, strategy and business model, and a materiality analysis. The content spans:

- Environment: climate change (E1) and alignment with the EU Green Taxonomy.
- Social: own workforce, affected communities, and customers.
- Governance: processes to identify and assess climate-related impacts, risks and opportunities; corporate culture and conduct policies; mechanisms to detect and investigate illicit behaviour; anti-corruption and anti-bribery measures; political influence and lobbying; supplier relationship management; payment practices; and tax transparency.

The introduction emphasizes enhanced transparency and continuity with prior frameworks (GRI, SASB, TCFD, IIRC) to aid comparability with 2023 reporting. It also notes inclusion of additional disclosures responsive to rating agencies, analysts, and other stakeholders.

structure.title: Basis for preparation
structure.heading: Basis for preparation
structure.start_phrase:
The contents of this report address the material 
issues identified in the 2024 Doble Materiality Study 
and in the requirements of Law 11/2018 on the 
disclosure of Non-financial and Diversity 
Information.
structure.summary:
- Basis for preparation: The report addresses material issues identified in the 2024 Double Materiality Study, complies with Spain’s Law 11/2018 on Non‑financial and Diversity Information and the ESRS, and aligns its structure to material ESRS standards. It also includes required disclosures under the EU Taxonomy (Regulation (EU) 2020/852 and Delegated Regulations 2021/2139 and 2021/2178).
- Scope and perimeter: Covers performance data for CaixaBank and its subsidiaries as of 31 December 2024, using the same consolidation perimeter as the financial statements (with entities listed in appendices). Any deviations from full perimeter are specifically indicated. The report includes analysis of impacts, risks and opportunities across prior and subsequent phases of the value chain based on the Double Materiality Study. Certain CapEx/Opex data are omitted for confidentiality; no other relevant information is omitted regarding IP, know‑how or innovation results.
- Time horizons: Material impacts, risks and opportunities are generally assessed as short term (1 year), medium term (1–5 years), and long term (>5 years). Different horizons may apply for climate risk scenarios and are disclosed when used.
- Estimation and uncertainty: Judgments and estimates are used where counterpart data are limited, prioritizing primary sources. Key areas include financed emissions (with estimated inputs such as property energy efficiency for mortgages), decarbonization pathways (use of proxies), Green Asset Ratio (counterparty/external data), and operational carbon footprint (estimates where needed). Assumptions may evolve; the Group commits to transparency and continuous improvement.
- Value chain disclosures by ESRS topic: 
  - Climate change (E1), downstream: decarbonization pathways and Scope 3, notably financed emissions.
  - Consumers and end users (S4), downstream: customer experience (NPS) and complaints.
  - Business conduct (G1), upstream: supplier relationship management.
- Changes and comparability: 2023 figures are presented for comparison. Methodological improvements were introduced in 2024 and are explained in their sections. The NFIS structure changed in 2024 to align with ESRS. No significant prior‑year errors required restatement.
- Other frameworks and references: The report also aligns with the UN Global Compact principles, SDGs, and the UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking. ESRS disclosures closely linked to corporate governance reference relevant management report sections in line with CNMV Circular 5/2013.
- Incorporation by reference: All ESRS and Law 11/2018 sustainability information is included in section 6 “Sustainability information” and section 8 “NFIS”.
- Verification: PwC provides limited assurance under Spanish auditing guidelines and ESRS for the NFIS, limited assurance under ISAE 3000 on selected UNEP FI PRB sections, and reasonable assurance under ISAE 3000 on certain sustainability indicators. Assurance reports are available in the annex.

structure.title: Sustainability governance
structure.heading: Sustainability governance
structure.start_phrase:
The bases of CaixaBank's governance model, in 
both its scopes —Governing Bodies in the strictest 
sense and Management Bodies—, are essentially 
defined in the Corporate Governance Policy and 
other related Policies, covering the companies 
making up the CaixaBank Group.
structure.summary:
- Describes CaixaBank’s sustainability governance model spanning Governing Bodies (Board and Board Committees) and Management Bodies, anchored in Corporate Governance Policy and ESG policies, to integrate material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) and create long-term stakeholder value aligned with ECB expectations and market best practice.
- Board of Directors: ultimate responsibility for defining, approving and overseeing the sustainability strategy, policies, objectives and KPIs; embeds ESG in strategic and operational plans, culture and stakeholder engagement; approved Sustainable Banking Plan 2022–2024 and new Sustainability Plan 2025–2027.
- Board composition and capabilities: diverse and suitable membership; ongoing sustainability training (including CSRD), information rights supported by the Sustainability Department; knowledge matrix used in suitability assessments.
- Board Committees and their ESG roles:
  - Appointments and Sustainability Committee: oversees sustainability actions and policy compliance; proposes ESG policies; reviews external ESG disclosures and key reports; monitors targets in the Sustainability Plan.
  - Risk Committee: proposes Group risk policy including sustainability risks; oversees risk reporting, controls and stress tests (e.g., climate, cybersecurity), DORA strategy and policy updates.
  - Audit and Control Committee: oversees preparation and completeness of sustainability reporting (NFIS/CSRD), and the effectiveness of internal controls for financial and non‑financial risks.
  - Remuneration Committee: aligns remuneration with ESG objectives and proposes ESG-linked variable pay.
- Management Bodies and execution:
  - Management Committee (via CEO): develops sustainability lines of action, approves and monitors ESG topics, and reports regularly to the Board.
  - Sustainability Committee (management body): monthly forum led by the Sustainability Director to steer the Sustainable Banking Plan, propose policies, approve market disclosures prior to Board submission, monitor NZBA pathways/metrics and RAF metrics.
  - Global Risk Committee: monthly management and monitoring of ESG risks, materiality, and supervisory feedback.
  - Sustainability Department: coordinates strategy, principles of action and ESG risk criteria; advises on partnerships.
  - Specialized internal committees: oversee specific IROs across functions.
- 2024 governance activity: extensive quarterly approvals and reviews across bodies, including updates to climate and nature statements, ESG risk policy, NZBA targets and governance, Green/Social Bond reports, CSRD implementation, double materiality study, Climate Report, customer and privacy reports, cybersecurity/DORA, and multiple corporate policy updates.
- Incentives: ESG factors embedded in variable remuneration for executive directors, identified staff, and from 2024 for the rest of the workforce.
- Policy and principles framework: comprehensive, updated suite covering ESG risk management, climate and nature statements, sustainability action principles, Human Rights Principles, Code of Ethics, criminal and regulatory compliance, anti‑corruption, conflicts of interest, AML/CFT, procurement and Supplier Code, tax, equality and people management, marketing and product governance, customer protection, privacy and information security, information reliability, and data governance.
- Sustainability due diligence:
  - General process integrates double materiality and stakeholder input; maps adverse impacts and embeds prevention, mitigation and monitoring across functions.
  - Human Rights due diligence (triennial, last in 2023 with third‑party verification) builds stakeholder-specific risk maps, verifies controls, and drives action plans; 24 recommendations in 2024 (majority completed) spanning employees (digital rights, inclusion), clients (sector criteria updates), suppliers (social audits, UNGC training), and community (Statement on Nature, social programs).
- Internal control over sustainability reporting:
  - Three lines of defence framework; Corporate policies on information reliability and data governance; COSO 2023 ICSR-aligned approach.
  - Risk assessment per report (inherent/residual risk, control environment, automation, frequency/complexity); key risks are disclosure adequacy and data errors.
  - Controls via ICNFR and report-level checks; continuous monitoring, remediation and regular reporting to Board, Audit, Risk, and Appointments & Sustainability Committees; Internal Audit independent oversight.

structure.title: Sustainability strategy and business model
structure.heading: Sustainability strategy and business model
structure.start_phrase: The CaixaBank Group's strategy and business model are significant contextual factors in defining which sustainable matters are material for the Group.
structure.summary:
- Strategy and business model: Sustainability is embedded in CaixaBank Group’s Strategic Plan via a dedicated Sustainability Plan. As a financial institution, the greatest sustainability impact comes through financing and investment, with a parallel focus on managing impacts from own operations. The Group prioritises decarbonising lending and investment portfolios (NZBA, NZAOA) while supporting clients’ transition with ESG advice and sustainable products.

- Universal banking-insurance model: Leader in Spain with growing presence in Portugal, offering segmented, omnichannel service (branches and digital) and a full suite of banking, investment, and insurance products that integrate sustainability. Emphasis on products that enable climate mitigation and adaptation (e.g., solar panel loans, green mortgages, energy‑efficient property financing, sustainability‑linked loans, renewables). In 2024, 45 new sustainable products were approved across financing, cards, and savings/insurance.

- Social purpose and inclusion: Strong microfinance and financial inclusion through MicroBank, rural access, financial education, and extensive social action via the CaixaBank volunteer network and collaboration with the “la Caixa” Foundation.

- Sustainable Banking Plan 2022–2024 (closing year 2024): Over 300 initiatives across governance, social impact, and climate transition. All targets achieved, including:
  - >€86.77bn mobilised in sustainable finance (vs. >€64bn target).
  - Maintenance of category “A” in a synthetic sustainability indicator.
  - Decarbonisation targets defined for 10 NZBA sectors toward 2030.
  - 484,522 MicroBank beneficiaries (vs. 413,300 target).
  - 43.4% women in managerial positions (vs. 43% target).
  - Advances in ESG governance, data, culture, risk integration, and expanded sustainable product offering.

- Sustainability Plan 2025–2027: Builds on prior plan, addressing inequality, climate change, biodiversity loss, conflicts, and demographic shifts. Two ambitions and five focus areas:
  - Advancing a more sustainable economy: invest in transition solutions (renewables, clean mobility, efficient buildings, industrial decarb) and sustainable intermediation; net-zero portfolio by 2050; support for businesses and issuers.
  - Supporting economic and social development: inclusion products, rural access, financial education and health, employability and entrepreneurship, and solutions for longevity (long-term savings and senior well-being).
  - Key targets: >€100bn sustainable finance mobilisation (2025–27), ~15% financial income from sustainable financing, 90% engagement with NZBA-sector clients, annual NZBA alignment reviews, 150,000 people supported into employment, 33% of customers aged 50–67 reached with long‑term savings and pensions, #1 NPS for senior customers among large listed Spanish banks, and leading ESG ratings vs. European peers.

- Value chain overview: Upstream (diverse suppliers, collaborators, funding providers including ECB), core operations (employees, training, omnichannel distribution), and downstream (20.3 million customers across retail, premier, private, business, and CIB). Supplier relationships emphasise ethics and ESG performance.

- Stakeholder engagement and integration: Continuous dialogue with customers, employees, shareholders/investors, suppliers, regulators/supervisors, ESG analysts, NGOs/foundations through surveys, forums, advisory bodies, and service channels. Findings feed into DAFO (SWOT), the Sustainability Plan, and the Strategic Plan. Governance bodies receive regular updates and oversee sustainability IROs.

- Double Materiality and IROs: Material ESRS topics identified include Climate Change (E1), Own workforce (S1), Affected communities (S3), Consumers and end users (S4), and Business conduct (G1), plus entity-specific Sustainable finance and Cybersecurity. Most material impacts arise upstream; own operations concentrate on workforce and conduct; downstream concentrates on climate, end users, sustainable finance, and cybersecurity. IROs span:
  - Climate: physical and transition risks to financed sectors; positive impacts from portfolio decarbonisation and exclusions; operational footprint management.
  - Workforce: fair work, diversity and inclusion, training/upskilling, engagement.
  - Consumers/end users: improved advice and education; risks of greenwashing and data protection.
  - Business conduct: ethics, tax contribution, regulatory compliance, AML/TF, transparency in public policy.
  - Sustainable finance: environmental/social financing and investment impacts and related controversy risks; opportunities from tailored sustainable offerings.
  - Cybersecurity: cyberattack and data leak risks across value chain.

- Resilience of strategy and model: Regular scenario analysis and stress testing (ICAAP/ILAAP, budgeting, Recovery Plan, EBA stress test, Fit‑for‑55 climate scenario, cyber resilience tests) inform strategic and risk decisions. Strong operational resilience aligned with EU DORA, including ICT risk governance, incident management, testing programs, third‑party ICT risk oversight, and an enhanced Business Continuity Management System. Continuous monitoring allows adaptation to evolving macro, regulatory, technological, and customer trends.

structure.title: Materiality Analysis
structure.heading: Materiality Analysis
structure.start_phrase:
CaixaBank annually conducts the Doble Materiality 
Study with the aim of identifying its main IROs, on 
which it focuses its sustainability strategy.
structure.summary:
- Purpose and scope: CaixaBank’s 2024 Double Materiality Study identifies key impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) to guide its sustainability strategy, applying CSRD, ESRS and EFRAG guidance across the full value chain and over short, medium, and long-term horizons.
- Dual perspective: Assesses both impact materiality (inside-out effects on people and environment) and financial materiality (outside-in sustainability risks and opportunities affecting financial performance). A topic can be material under one or both perspectives.
- Governance and controls: The study follows established non-financial reporting controls, adds alignment checks with internal risk processes, and is reviewed/approved by Management, the Board, and relevant Board committees.
- Four-phase methodology:
  1) Context analysis: Exhaustive review of internal documents (strategy, policies, risk processes, due diligence, reputational analysis) and external sources (CSRD/ESRS, supervisors, ESG ratings, WEF, sector trends).
  2) Identification: Mapped IROs to operations/value chain with business area input; validated by responsible departments; recognized interdependencies; linked IROs to value chain segments; 118 IROs identified and grouped per ESRS-1 AR 16.
  3) Assessment: Separate evaluations for current vs. potential impacts and for risks vs. opportunities using 1–5 scales.
     - Impact materiality variables: scope, scale, likelihood (for potential), and remediability (for negatives); supported by qualitative validation with responsible areas and review of management tools.
     - Financial materiality: Likelihood and magnitude (in euros), aligned with the corporate risk catalogue, ESG risk materiality, and risk appetite; opportunities informed by internal estimates and market analysis.
     - Timeframes: Short (≤1 year), medium (1–5 years), long (>5 years). Control environment considered as mitigation.
  4) Results and thresholds: Quantified scores (1–5); separate thresholds for impact and financial materiality. Impact threshold based on top 25% of scores. Financial thresholds aligned with risk frameworks. Outcome: 32 material IROs grouped into 7 topics and 16 subtopics.
- Stakeholder engagement: 1,045 surveys, 2 focus groups, and 27 interviews across 10 stakeholder groups (employees, customers, investors, suppliers, regulators, media, NGOs, sustainability leaders, academia, society). Stakeholders see strongest positive impacts in privacy/data protection, cybersecurity/information security, and human rights; potential negatives in decarbonisation of portfolios, value offer, responsible marketing/customer satisfaction, and anti-corruption/bribery.
- Materiality matrix (topic level): Very high/high materiality for Climate change; Own workforce; Affected communities; Consumers and end users; Business conduct; Sustainable finance; Cybersecurity and information security. Non-material ESRS topics in 2024: Pollution (E2), Water and marine resources (E3), Biodiversity and ecosystems (E4), Circular economy (E5), and Workers in the value chain (S2), reflecting limited direct operational impact for a bank; ongoing nature-related assessment (GBS/ENCORE, heatmaps) may change future conclusions.
- Strategic alignment: Sustainability is a core pillar of the 2025–2027 Strategic Plan (“Differential positioning in ESG”). Material topics map to strategic pillars on growth, business transformation/investment, and ESG leadership, embedding IRO management into overall strategy.
- Climate change deep-dive:
  - Impact identification: Focus on financed emissions (Scope 3 Category 15); sectors with highest inside-out materiality include oil & gas, electricity, iron & steel, automotive, real estate, agriculture/livestock; coal treated as material; aluminium/cement have limited exposure. Positive impacts recognized from not financing/investing in high-emitting sectors and from reducing operational footprint.
  - Commitments: NZBA founding member; sectoral 2030 decarbonisation targets and net-zero by 2050.
  - Risk identification: Physical (acute/chronic) and transition risks mapped to credit, market, operational, liquidity, reputational, and strategic risks; sectoral focus supported by external advisors; physical risk assessed via asset and collateral locations.
  - Opportunities: Growth in sustainable lending (green loans, SLLs, energy efficiency), green bonds, customer investment products, enhanced reputation, and regulatory alignment/transparency.

nodes.title: Climate change
nodes.heading: 1 Climate change
nodes.start_phrase: Accelerating the transition to a neutral carbon economy that encourages sustainable development and is socially inclusive is essential, in CaixaBank’s view.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on accelerating a socially inclusive transition to a carbon‑neutral economy, aligned with the Paris Agreement (COP21) and UN Sustainable Development Goals.
- Emphasis on the pivotal role of financial institutions in achieving climate objectives through both internal operations and influence across customers, investees, partners, and the value chain.
- CaixaBank’s commitments: founding member of the Net‑Zero Banking Alliance; public pledge to achieve net‑zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.
- Portfolio decarbonisation positioned as a core driver of the Group’s sustainability strategy, alongside financing and investing in sustainable projects.
- Recognition that climate-related risks can materially affect the economy and CaixaBank’s activities, with established processes to identify, assess, and manage climate risks and opportunities.

nodes.title: Description of the processes to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities related to climate change
nodes.heading: 1.1 Description of the processes to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities related to climate change
nodes.start_phrase: According to science, the main cause of climate change are the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions produced directly or indirectly by human activity.
nodes.summary:
- Focus of assessment: CaixaBank evaluates climate-related impacts primarily through financed emissions (Scope 3, Category 15), analyzing its lending and investment portfolio to identify high CO2eq-intensity sectors.
- Sectoral materiality: High inside-out materiality in oil and gas, electricity, iron and steel, automotive, real estate (commercial and residential), and agriculture/livestock; aluminium and cement have limited exposure; coal is considered material for impact despite NACE underestimation (e.g., coal-based power generation).
- Decarbonization stance: Although financing these sectors could have negative impacts, CaixaBank deems them not material due to its decarbonization strategy, NZBA commitment, 2030 sector targets, and net-zero by 2050; material impacts emphasized as positive outcomes from not financing/investing in high-carbon sectors.
- Operational footprint: The bank also identifies material impacts related to its own operational carbon footprint and implements actions to reduce it.
- 2024 Double Materiality Study highlights:
  - Contribution to decarbonization by avoiding finance for highly carbon-intensive sectors.
  - Emissions reduction by not investing in heavily polluting sectors or those failing minimum decarbonization standards.
  - Environmental impact from the bank’s operational footprint.
  - Internal footprint reduction driven by action plans with improvements and recommendations.
- Risk identification framework: Climate risks are assessed within the ESG risk materiality process, which feeds the Double Materiality Study.
- Risk taxonomy and drivers:
  - Physical risks: chronic (shifting climate patterns, temperature, rainfall, sea-level rise) and severe (more frequent/intense extreme events like hurricanes, floods).
  - Transition risks: policy/legal (regulatory changes), technological (new efficient alternatives, obsolescence), and market (shifts in preferences and market dynamics).
- Risk impact determinants: The effect depends on event probability and intensity, and on companies’ capacity to anticipate and respond.

nodes.title: Identification and assessment of climate change impacts
nodes.heading: 1.1.1 Identification and assessment of climate change impacts
nodes.start_phrase: According to science, the main cause of climate change are the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions produced directly or indirectly by human activity.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Outlines CaixaBank’s processes for identifying and assessing material climate-related impacts, risks, and opportunities, feeding into the 2024 Double Materiality Study and ESG risk materiality assessment.

- Impact identification and assessment:
  - Focus on financed emissions (Scope 3, Category 15) to determine inside-out materiality across the lending and investment portfolio.
  - High-emitting, material sectors (NACE): oil and gas, electricity, iron and steel, automotive, real estate (commercial and residential), agriculture and livestock. Aluminium and cement have limited exposure and are not considered material. Coal is deemed material by impact despite NACE underestimation (e.g., coal-based power generation).
  - Although financing these sectors could create negative impacts, CaixaBank deems them non-material given its decarbonisation strategy, NZBA commitment, sectoral 2030 targets, and net-zero by 2050. The material impacts highlighted are the positive effects of not financing/investing in high-carbon sectors.
  - Operational footprint impacts are also recognized.
  - Double Materiality Study 2024 impact highlights:
    - Contribution to decarbonisation by not financing highly carbon‑intensive sectors.
    - Emission reductions by not investing in heavily polluting sectors or those failing minimum decarbonisation standards.
    - Environmental impacts from the bank’s operational carbon footprint.
    - Internal footprint reduction promoted through action plans with improvements and recommendations.

- Risk and opportunity identification and assessment:
  - Conducted within the ESG risk materiality framework, using a qualitative assessment of how ESG factors affect traditional risk types.
  - Climate risks classified as:
    - Physical risks: chronic (e.g., shifting temperature/rainfall patterns, sea-level rise) and severe (e.g., more frequent/intense hurricanes, floods, tornadoes), with potential damage to assets, disruptions to production/supply chains, and reduced productivity.
    - Transition risks: policy/legal changes, technological shifts (efficiency/obsolescence), and market changes (consumer preferences, market dynamics).
  - Risk impact depends on the likelihood and severity of events and companies’ capacity to anticipate and respond.

nodes.title: Identification and assessment of climate change risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 1.1.2 Identification and assessment of climate change risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: The identification of climate risks is carried out within the framework of the assessment of the materiality of sustainability (ESG) risks, which has been used as input in the Doble Materiality Study.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Explains CaixaBank’s processes to identify and assess climate-related material impacts, risks, and opportunities across its value chain, focusing on financed emissions and portfolio exposure.

- Impact identification (inside-out):
  - Focuses on financed footprint (Scope 3, Category 15) to locate high CO2eq intensity sectors per NACE.
  - Material sectors: oil & gas, electricity, iron & steel, automotive, real estate (commercial and residential), agriculture & livestock; coal treated as material despite under-capture in NACE; aluminium and cement deemed non-material due to limited exposure.
  - Despite potential negative impacts from exposure to high-emitting sectors, CaixaBank frames material impacts as positive due to its decarbonisation strategy, NZBA commitments, 2030 sector targets, and net-zero by 2050.
  - Operational footprint impacts also identified.
  - 2024 Doble Materiality Study highlights: positive impact from not financing/investing in high-carbon sectors, environmental impact from operational footprint, and internal footprint reduction via action plans.

- Risk and opportunity assessment (outside-in):
  - Climate risks defined as physical (chronic and acute) and transition (policy/legal, technology, market).
  - Method: qualitative ESG risk materiality assessment feeding the Doble Materiality Study; sector screening for higher transition risk with external advisers; NZBA used to set targets/manage risk; physical risk assessed via locations of corporate assets and collateral.
  - Mapping to risk types:
    - Credit: PD and collateral value affected by both physical and transition drivers; stranded assets risk.
    - Market: price and maturity changes from extreme events and transition repricing.
    - Operational: service interruption, asset damage; heightened legal/compliance risk around sustainable products and disclosures.
    - Liquidity: deposit outflows post-physical events; potential investor divestment if misaligned with transition; liquidity buffers sensitive to policy/temperature shifts.
    - Reputational: stakeholder perceptions regarding decarbonisation efforts, exposures to ESG controversies.
    - Business/strategic: profitability and strategy resilience affected by policy/market shifts; GDP impacts from physical events.
  - Opportunities: growth in sustainable finance (sustainability-linked and green lending, renewables, energy-efficient buildings/retrofits, eco-mobility), green bonds, client investment products aligned to climate action, reputational benefits, and transparency/regulatory alignment. A material opportunity is the mobilisation of sustainable finance.

- Scenario analysis:
  - Uses NGFS scenarios: orderly transition (base case), disorderly transition, and Hot House World; aligns orderly with IPCC SSP1-2.6 and monitors compatibility with SSP2-4.5 given evolving science.
  - Under orderly transition, impacts concentrate in long-term credit portfolios; sectoral transition risk highest for agriculture, electricity, oil & gas, transport, materials, mining/metallurgy; priority focus on coal-power and oil & gas; real estate notable due to portfolio weight.
  - Physical risk to portfolio assessed as moderate overall; mortgage physical risk not material in short/medium term; granular hotspot and sector analyses applied.
  - Market risk low given small trading book; operational residual risk low but medium-term transition conduct/compliance risk may rise; reputational risk controlled short term but increases over time; liquidity risk not material short term; business profitability risk mitigated by the 2025–2027 Sustainability Plan and transition-focused strategy.

- Materiality conclusion:
  - Only credit risk is currently material for climate risk (both transition and physical) across scenarios, especially over the medium to long term.
  - Management focus is therefore on prudential credit risk, integrating sector priorities, client-level analyses, and energy efficiency data (e.g., mortgages).

- Overall takeaway:
  - CaixaBank combines financed-emission impact assessment, ESG risk materiality, location-based physical risk analysis, NGFS-aligned scenario testing, and NZBA target setting to manage climate risks and capture opportunities, with a strategic emphasis on decarbonisation and sustainable finance mobilisation.

nodes.title: Climate change risk management
nodes.heading: 1.2 Climate change risk management
nodes.start_phrase: Based on the assessment of the materiality of ESG risks ( ä see section "Materiality Analysis" ), CaixaBank has prioritised managing climate risks.
nodes.summary:
- CaixaBank prioritizes climate risk management based on its ESG materiality assessment.
- A Corporate Sustainability/ESG Risk Management Policy incorporates climate risk and is governed within the ESG risk governance framework.
- Practices align with regulatory standards and market best practices, notably the ECB’s 2020 Guide on climate-related and environmental risks, with action plans to meet supervisory expectations by end-2024.
- A scenario measurement and analysis framework has been developed to assess climate risk impacts on credit risk.
- Analysis focuses on credit portfolios of legal entities, reflecting that under an orderly transition scenario the main climate impacts materialize in credit risk, supported by a heat map in the risk identification section.
- The framework enhances comprehensive climate risk assessment and quantifies potential impacts on financial results and operations.
- It combines qualitative scenario analysis with a quantitative measurement and monitoring approach.

nodes.title: Scenario measurement and analysis framework
nodes.heading: 1.2.1 Scenario measurement and analysis framework
nodes.start_phrase: CaixaBank has developed a framework for measuring and analysing scenarios to measure the impact of climate risk on credit risk.
nodes.summary:
- CaixaBank prioritizes managing climate-related risks based on its ESG materiality assessment.
- It has a Corporate Sustainability/ESG Risk Management Policy that integrates climate risk, supported by an ESG risk governance framework.
- The approach aligns with regulatory standards and market best practices, notably the ECB’s 2020 Guide on climate and environmental risks; action plans aim for full alignment by end-2024.
- A scenario measurement and analysis framework has been developed to assess climate risk impacts on credit risk.
- The materiality assessment indicates that, under an orderly transition scenario, climate impacts are concentrated in credit risk, particularly within corporate/legal entity portfolios.
- The framework strengthens overall climate risk assessment and quantifies potential impacts on financial results and operations.
- It combines qualitative scenario analysis with a quantitative measurement and monitoring system.

nodes.title: Qualitative scenario analysis
nodes.heading: 1.2.1.1 Qualitative scenario analysis
nodes.start_phrase: CaixaBank regularly carries out an assessment of the main drivers of transition risk and of how the corporate and mortgage portfolio performs assuming the predictions of the central scenario (orderly transition).
nodes.summary:
- Describes CaixaBank’s qualitative scenario analysis of climate-related risks, regularly assessing transition risk drivers and performance of corporate (and, by reference, mortgage) portfolios under an orderly transition central scenario.
- For the corporate portfolio, outlines use of heat maps to evaluate transition risks, initially targeting sectors with material portfolio risk and high emissions: oil and gas, electricity, automotive, aviation, naval, residential and commercial real estate, cement, iron and steel, aluminium, and agriculture.
- Details analysis across multiple time horizons (2025, 2030, 2040, 2050) aligned with CaixaBank’s decarbonisation commitments and 1.5°C scenarios in net‑zero‑by‑2050 geographies.
- Notes granular assessment at NACE activity level across sector value chains to identify key risk variables and impacts.
- Addresses physical risk by linking climate event exposure to company financials based on location and activity, highlighting agriculture (drought), construction (heat waves), and transport (coastal floods) as most impacted, with construction the most exposed among CaixaBank’s sectors.
- States that quantitative analyses on these portfolios corroborate the qualitative findings and refers to a dedicated section on the quantitative framework for measuring and monitoring financial impacts of physical and transition risks.

nodes.title: Corporate portfolio
nodes.heading: 1.2.1.1.1 Corporate portfolio
nodes.start_phrase: In the corporate portfolio, CaixaBank conducts qualitative scenario analyses for climate risks in the form of heat maps.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: CaixaBank conducts qualitative scenario analyses to assess climate-related transition and physical risks, focusing on how the corporate (and by reference, mortgage) portfolios perform under an orderly transition central scenario aligned with its decarbonisation commitments.
- Methodology: Uses sectoral heat maps with granular NACE-level analysis across the value chain, evaluated over multiple time horizons (2025, 2030, 2040, 2050) under 1.5°C pathways in geographies targeting net-zero by 2050.
- Transition risk focus: Identifies segments most affected within emission‑intensive sectors—oil & gas, electricity, automotive, aviation, naval, residential and commercial real estate, cement, iron & steel, aluminium, and agriculture—mapping the level of impact against portfolio exposure.
- Physical risk focus: Assesses how climate events affect companies’ financials based on location and activity; highlights agriculture (droughts), construction (heat waves), and transport (coastal floods) as most impacted, with construction the most exposed among CaixaBank’s sectors.
- Validation: Notes that quantitative analyses of these portfolios corroborate the qualitative findings, with reference to a dedicated quantitative framework section.
- Sector risk mapping (illustrative outcomes): High transition risk for fossil fuel combustion, electricity, transport, iron & steel, aluminium, cement, agriculture/livestock/fishing, coal, and mining/metallurgy; average for real estate, infrastructure, services, and tourism; low for healthcare, technology/communications, other utilities, consumption, discretionary consumption, and industry/manufacture; finance marked as N/A.
- Portfolio view: Presents a visual map (bubble chart) positioning sectors by portfolio share and transition risk impact, enabling prioritization of risk management actions.

nodes.title: Mortgage portfolio
nodes.heading: 1.2.1.1.2 Mortgage portfolio
nodes.start_phrase: With regard to the mortgage portfolio, CaixaBank monitors the evolution of energy performance certificates (EPC) of financed households with the aim of being aware of their exposure to transition risks .
nodes.summary:
- Focus: CaixaBank’s mortgage portfolio and its exposure to climate-related risks, with emphasis on energy performance certificates (EPCs).
- Transition risk monitoring: Since 2021, CaixaBank tracks EPCs for financed homes using actual certificates where available and proxies otherwise.
- Sources of transition risk:
  - Regulatory: EU Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) requirements, including CO2-neutral new builds from 2030 and upgrades of EPC “G” homes to “F” by 2030 and to “E” by 2033.
  - Market: Growing preference and potentially higher valuations for energy-efficient properties, which may depress prices of lower-rated homes.
- Portfolio trends and expectations:
  - Progressive improvement in overall portfolio energy efficiency as older, less efficient properties mature and as financing of A/B-rated homes increases.
  - Comparison provided between existing stock and 2024 new production by EPC rating, indicating better efficiency in new production.
- Data quality enhancement: An agreement with an external provider increased the share of contracts with actual EPCs, reducing reliance on proxies; distribution by certificate type is presented.
- Physical risk assessment: Despite Spain’s higher exposure to climate physical risks, a qualitative review deems mortgage portfolio impact low, as collateral is largely in lower-risk urban areas.
- Reporting visuals: Charts show EPC rating distribution across the portfolio, and the evolution from Dec-23 to Dec-24 in terms of estimated collateral and information availability.

nodes.title: Quantitative framework for measurement and monitoring of financial impacts of physical and transition risks
nodes.heading: 1.2.1.2 Quantitative framework for measurement and monitoring of financial impacts of physical and transition risks
nodes.start_phrase: CaixaBank has a quantitative framework in place for measuring the impact of climate risks on credit risk.
nodes.summary:
- Describes CaixaBank’s quantitative framework to measure and monitor how climate-related physical and transition risks affect credit risk, supporting materiality assessment and coherent risk management.
- Scope covers a wide range of physical hazards (e.g., floods, fires, prolonged droughts) and transition risks from the shift to a low‑carbon economy.
- Assesses impacts on two credit risk parameters: probability of default (PD) and loss given default (LGD).
- Physical risk channels: PD increases due to business interruptions causing income loss or asset damage; LGD rises via declines in mortgage collateral values from climate-related damage.
- Transition risk channels: PD increases due to higher costs (emissions costs, required CAPEX) and potential revenue reductions; LGD increases when collateral is less energy‑efficient than evolving EU standards, lowering its value.
- Quantification relies primarily on scenario analyses to project and track PD and LGD impacts over time.

nodes.title: Measurement of the physical risk
nodes.heading: 1.2.1.2.1 Measurement of the physical risk
nodes.start_phrase: The method designed to identify the exposures subject to physical risk is based on projecting climate events in the geographies where CaixaBank has exposure and the impact that these can have on the Group's financial results and operations.
nodes.summary:
- Describes CaixaBank’s methodology for measuring physical climate risk by projecting hazards (wildfires, river/coastal flooding, droughts, heat waves) across geographies of exposure.
- Builds postcode-level probability maps for each hazard under three NGFS-aligned scenarios (orderly, disorderly, hot house world) and multiple timeframes, with long-term projections to 2050 using official international and national data.
- Cross-references these maps with the mortgage portfolio and corporate locations to assign hazard probabilities to each property and non-financial company, producing a granular view of asset vulnerability.
- Quantifies impacts on credit risk parameters:
  - Probability of Default (PD): assesses sectoral and borrower-level credit quality impacts from hazard severity and exposure.
  - Loss Given Default (LGD): estimates collateral value reductions via haircuts reflecting physical risk impacts on property appraisals.
- Measures transition risk by evaluating corporate credit impacts from emissions profiles, carbon price trajectories, decarbonization pathways, required investments, and cost pressures on volumes and margins; also considers reduced attractiveness of energy-inefficient properties as mortgage collateral.
- Notes that current scenario analyses show limited impact on the lending portfolio for both physical and transition risks, while highlighting ongoing data and scenario-design challenges.
- Commits to continuous methodological and data improvements to strengthen the climate risk management framework and inform risk policy adjustments.

nodes.title: Measurement of transition risk
nodes.heading: 1.2.1.2.2 Measurement of transition risk
nodes.start_phrase: The transition risk's assessment allows quantifying its impact on the credit quality of companies, considering key factors such as the carbon emissions, price evolution, decarbonisation pathways and investments required for the transition.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: CaixaBank’s framework for measuring climate-related physical and transition risks and their integration into credit risk management.
- Physical risk methodology:
  - Projects climate events (forest fires, river/coastal flooding, droughts, heat waves) across geographies of exposure.
  - Builds probability-of-occurrence maps by postcode under NGFS scenarios (orderly, disorderly, hot house) with long-term horizons to 2050.
  - Uses data from international and national official bodies to ensure reliability and alignment with global standards.
  - Cross-references maps with the mortgage portfolio and corporate locations to assign event probabilities to each asset and obtain a detailed view of vulnerability.
- Credit risk impact quantification:
  - Probability of Default (PD): estimates sectoral and obligor-level impacts based on hazard severity and how events like prolonged droughts or extreme heat affect operations and asset stability.
  - Loss Given Default (LGD): applies haircuts to collateral appraisal values to capture the effect of physical risks on guarantee values.
- Transition risk methodology:
  - Assesses impacts on companies’ credit quality considering emissions profiles, carbon price evolution, decarbonization pathways, and required transition investments.
  - Evaluates effects of rising production costs on business volumes and margins.
  - Estimates potential devaluation of less energy-efficient properties used as mortgage collateral.
- Findings and constraints:
  - Scenario analyses to date indicate limited impacts from both physical and transition risks on the lending portfolio.
  - Notes methodological challenges related to data availability and scenario design, which are evolving.
- Ongoing enhancement:
  - Continuous improvement of analytical and methodological capabilities to refine climate risk measurement and strengthen the risk management framework over time.

nodes.title: Main assumptions of the quantitative framework for measurement and monitoring
nodes.heading: 1.2.1.2.3 Main assumptions of the quantitative framework for measurement and monitoring
nodes.start_phrase: In order to measure and project the climate risk impacts in the credit risk, the assumptions have a conservative approach, with the aim of guaranteeing that the results show unfavourable but plausible scenarios.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and approach: Defines the main assumptions of a conservative quantitative framework to measure and project climate-related impacts on credit risk, aiming to produce unfavorable but plausible results.
- Scenario set: Relies on NGFS climate scenarios to capture differing evolutions of physical risks, transition policies, technology, and preferences.
  - Net Zero 2050 (Orderly Transition): Immediate, ambitious policies and innovation; minimal sustainable use of carbon dioxide removal; net CO₂ emissions reach zero around 2050; ≥50% chance of limiting warming to below 1.5°C with no/low overshoot (<0.1°C); relatively low physical risks, high transition risks.
  - Delayed Transition (Disorderly): Emissions do not fall until 2030; stronger, later policies with uneven global action; limited CDR availability drives higher carbon prices; temporary overshoot of the carbon budget followed by rapid declines to secure a 67% chance of staying below 2°C; higher physical and transition risks than an orderly path.
  - Current Policies (Hot house world): Only existing policies persist; emissions rise until ~2080; ~3°C warming leads to severe, potentially irreversible physical impacts, including sea-level rise; frames long-term physical risk exposure.
- Time horizons and methodology: Assesses both physical and transition risks over short-, medium-, and long-term horizons up to 2050. Physical impacts originally modeled for 2080 are brought forward to 2050 (in line with the ECB 2022 stress test) to improve comparability across scenarios and support clearer, more actionable risk planning amid uncertainty.
- Alignment note: Scenarios align with those used in climate risk materiality assessments but do not match CSRD timeframes.

nodes.title: Other assumptions
nodes.heading: 1.2.1.2.3.1 Other assumptions
nodes.start_phrase: Static balance sheet: The long-term analysis assumes that CaixaBank's balance sheet remains static, that is, that the lending portfolio's composition will not change significantly in terms of exposure to climate risks.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines conservative assumptions used in CaixaBank’s long-term climate risk analysis:
  - Static balance sheet: portfolio composition is assumed unchanged, excluding proactive portfolio rebalancing (e.g., diversification or shifts away from vulnerable sectors/geographies).
  - Static EPCs: energy performance certificates for mortgaged properties are assumed not to improve over time, avoiding overestimation of benefits from energy efficiency upgrades.
- Describes the quantitative framework’s data sources for measuring and projecting climate risks:
  - Customer information:
    - Internal by counterparty: questionnaires on carbon footprint, ESG exclusions, transition plans, impact and mitigation assessments.
    - Internal by physical asset: environmental due diligence for project/asset/corporate finance; EPCs for new mortgages.
    - Public: client reports and information on environmental litigation.
  - External data providers and public institutions: ESG rating agencies; UNEP FI, IPCC, IEA, PIK, INE; NGFS; PCAF; and the EU Copernicus Earth Observation Programme.

nodes.title: Data source used in the measurement
nodes.heading: 1.2.1.2.3.2 Data source used in the measurement
nodes.start_phrase: In order to measure the impact of risks related to climate change, the quantitative framework for measuring and projecting climate risks employs different data sources:
nodes.summary:
- Presents conservative assumptions used in CaixaBank’s long‑term climate risk analysis:
  - Static balance sheet: portfolio composition assumed unchanged, excluding potential proactive portfolio management (diversification, asset mix shifts) to reduce exposure to vulnerable sectors/geographies; ensures results don’t rely on uncertain future actions.
  - Static EPCs: properties’ energy performance certificates assumed not to improve over time, avoiding overestimation of benefits from energy-efficiency investments and yielding a more conservative risk estimate.
- Describes data sources feeding the quantitative framework for measuring and projecting climate risks:
  - Customer information:
    - Internal by counterparty: carbon footprint, ESG exclusions, transition plans, impact assessments, and mitigation plans gathered during onboarding.
    - Internal by physical asset: environmental due diligence for project/asset finance and corporate projects; EPCs collected for new mortgages.
    - Public: customer reports and information on environmental lawsuits.
  - External providers and public bodies: ESG rating agencies; UNEP FI, IPCC, IEA, PIK, INE; NGFS; PCAF; and the EU’s Copernicus Earth Observation Programme.

nodes.title: Limitations of the measurement and assessment
nodes.heading: 1.2.1.2.4 Limitations of the measurement and assessment
nodes.start_phrase: Due to the nature of the risks linked to climate change, measuring and projecting their impacts on the credit risk has a series of limitations:
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines the key constraints in measuring and projecting climate change impacts on credit risk: limited and inconsistent historical data linking climate events to credit performance; the need for forward-looking tools beyond past experience; uncertainty about when and how climate change will affect different sectors and geographies; the long-term horizon of climate risks; reliance on scenario assumptions (e.g., future policies) that add uncertainty; challenges integrating non-linear, systemic climate effects into existing credit risk models; and shortcomings in data quality and availability. In response, CaixaBank identifies data availability as a primary focus area and is developing a comprehensive sustainability data model under its Sustainability Plan to meet sustainability data needs and strengthen analyses.

nodes.title: Sensitivity to climate risk
nodes.heading: 1.2.1.2.5 Sensitivity to climate risk
nodes.start_phrase: CaixaBank identifies the exposures subject to physical risk and transition risk based on the aforementioned methodology and under the orderly transition scenario.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scenario: Presents CaixaBank’s assessment of lending portfolio sensitivity to climate risk under an “orderly transition” scenario, used as the base for materiality and aligned with EU policy expectations and the bank’s commitments.
- Methodology backbone: Uses a climate risk heatmap to identify exposures subject to physical (acute and chronic) and transition risks, providing a comprehensive view across sectors and geographies.
- Physical risk by sector: Details sectoral exposures sensitive to chronic, acute, and combined events. Coverage spans NACE sectors A–H, L, and real estate-related exposures, including:
  - Loans collateralised by residential property with the largest amount flagged for physical risk (notably split across chronic, acute, and both).
  - Loans collateralised by commercial property, repossessed collateral, and other corporate sectors (manufacturing, utilities, construction, wholesale/retail, transport, etc.).
- Physical risk by geography (NUTS): Breaks down exposures across Spanish provinces and Portuguese NUTS 3 regions, showing sensitivity to chronic, acute, and combined events and share of total. Highlights material concentrations in:
  - Spain: Barcelona, Seville, Malaga, Valencia, Murcia, Cadiz, Balearic Islands (Ibiza/Formentera, Majorca), and Canary Islands (Gran Canaria, Tenerife, Lanzarote), among others.
  - Portugal: Greater Lisbon, Porto metropolitan area, Aveiro, Coimbra, Leiria, Viseu Dão Lafões, Algarve, and other regions.
- Important notes and scope: Figures correspond to the CaixaBank Group’s prudential scope. Sector/guarantee breakdowns can duplicate exposures; NUTS-based property location data are unique, so the two views are not directly reconcilable.
- Transition risk exposure: Identifies exposures to sectors that highly contribute to climate change, based on CaixaBank’s transition risk heatmap and functional criteria. Notable exposures include:
  - Manufacturing, electricity/gas/steam, transportation/storage, wholesale/retail, agriculture, mining; plus real-estate–backed lending:
    - Loans collateralised by residential property (largest transition-risk exposure),
    - Loans collateralised by commercial property,
    - Repossessed collateral.
  - Note: These amounts differ from Information of Prudential Relevance because only high-risk non-financial companies identified in the heatmap are included.
- Energy efficiency of collateral: Provides distribution of exposures by estimated energy consumption bands (kWh/m²) and EPC labels (A–G), including a significant portion without EPC labels, with separate views for:
  - Commercial real estate–backed loans,
  - Residential mortgage–backed loans,
  - Repossessed residential and commercial properties.
- Overall takeaway: The section quantifies and localizes climate-related sensitivities across the lending book—by sector, collateral type, and region—covering both physical (acute/chronic) and transition risks, and links transition risk in real estate to collateral energy performance.

nodes.title: Analysis of scenarios and Stress test
nodes.heading: 1.2.1.2.6 Analysis of scenarios and Stress test
nodes.start_phrase: The quantitative measurement framework is the basis for integrating climate risk in both capital requirements and the severely adverse scenario for the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP).
nodes.summary:
- Describes the bank’s quantitative framework for integrating climate risk into capital requirements and the ICAAP severely adverse scenario.
- Notes first-time inclusion (Dec 2023 reference date) of capital requirements for climate risk in ICAAP, using adverse scenarios: “orderly transition” for transition risk and “Hot House World” for physical risk, reflecting a conservative stance.
- Confirms a 3-year ICAAP horizon aligned with financial planning and stress testing methodologies.
- Concludes that climate risks have an immaterial impact on economic capital.
- Extends the methodology to quantify exposures affecting liquidity risk, incorporating the impact into the ILAAP.
- Reports CaixaBank’s participation (end-2023 to early-2024) in the EBA’s one-off Fit‑for‑55 climate risk scenario analysis assessing system-wide resilience and support for the green transition under stress (baseline, AD1, AD2).
- Summarizes EBA results (disclosed end‑2024): transition risk losses alone do not threaten financial stability, but could rise notably when combined with macroeconomic stress; major institutions are well capitalized, diversified, and able to hedge/absorb losses.
- Details scenario design: Baseline implements Fit‑for‑55 (55% emissions cut by 2030 vs. 1990 and net zero by 2050) with immediate transition costs (3.7 billion euros energy investments 2022–2030 and a 14.5 pp reduction in fossil fuel consumption); AD1 adds a sudden “run‑on‑brown” asset price correction; AD2 layers in macroeconomic stress akin to EBA stress tests.

nodes.title: Impact of climate change on the Financial Statements
nodes.heading: 1.3 Impact of climate change on the Financial Statements
nodes.start_phrase: As previously mentioned, CaixaBank is exposed to risks associated with climate change mainly via the financing of sectors exposed to extreme weather or those more intensive in CO2 emissions.
nodes.summary:
- The document analyzes how climate change risks could affect CaixaBank’s financial statements, primarily through exposure to carbon‑intensive or weather‑sensitive sectors and the knock‑on effects on households’ and companies’ ability to invest, save, and meet payment obligations.
- Identified financial statement impacts focus on:
  - Net interest income: potential pressure if clients’ investment capacity weakens.
  - Allowances for insolvency risk: higher provisions driven by deteriorated borrower performance and declines in collateral values.
  - Capital adequacy: a slight potential reduction due to higher provisions and lower income/returns.
- Despite these risks, CaixaBank’s scenario analysis indicates limited impacts on the lending portfolio from both transition and physical climate risks.
- Risk management and mitigation measures include:
  - Close monitoring and client engagement with action plans to support transition.
  - Adjusting the portfolio mix toward less GHG‑intensive clients and sectors (aligned with NZBA).
  - Financing opportunities tied to adaptation and the energy transition, leveraging growing demand for sustainable finance.
- Outlook on net interest income: no negative impact expected in the short to medium term due to portfolio flexibility and new sustainable finance revenue streams.
- Provisioning approach: downside scenarios incorporate climate‑related macro headwinds (e.g., higher production and commodity costs) that could weigh on productivity and GDP, informing expected credit loss calculations.
- Scenario weightings applied in Spain and Portugal for 2022–2024 are consistent at 60% baseline, 20% upside, and 20% downside.

nodes.title: Impact on the net interest income
nodes.heading: 1.3.1 Impact on the net interest income
nodes.start_phrase: A negative impact on the net interest income caused by the climate risk is not expected in the medium/short term.
nodes.summary:
- The document analyzes how climate change risks could affect CaixaBank’s financial statements, primarily through exposure to high CO2-emitting and weather-sensitive sectors.
- It explains that climate risks may weaken households’ and companies’ financial positions, potentially impacting their payment capacity, savings, and investment, which in turn affects the bank.
- Identified income statement impacts:
  - Net interest income: potential reduction if clients’ investment capacity declines.
  - Allowances for insolvency risk: potential increase due to higher credit risk and collateral value losses from climate-related events.
- These effects could slightly reduce capital adequacy ratios via higher provisions and lower earnings.
- Scenario analysis within CaixaBank’s risk framework indicates limited impact on the lending portfolio from both transition and physical risks.
- Risk management measures include:
  - Action plans and customer engagement to support transition.
  - Adjusting the portfolio mix toward lower-risk, less GHG-intensive exposures (aligned with NZBA commitments).
  - Financing opportunities tied to adaptation and the energy transition to diversify income.
- Net interest income outlook: no negative impact expected in the short/medium term due to portfolio flexibility and growth in sustainable finance.
- Provisions methodology: downside scenarios incorporate macro effects consistent with exacerbated climate risk (e.g., higher production and commodity costs leading to lower productivity and GDP).
- Scenario weightings used for Spain and Portugal across 2022–2024 are stable at 60% baseline, 20% upside, 20% downside.

nodes.title: Impact on the calculation of allowances for insolvency risk
nodes.heading: 1.3.2 Impact on the calculation of allowances for insolvency risk
nodes.start_phrase: The downside range of variables used to calculate provisions includes deficiencies in structural reforms leading —together with other macroeconomic dynamics— to drops in productivity and thus in GDP.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: How climate change risks could affect CaixaBank’s financial statements.
- Risk channels: Exposure through financing of sectors vulnerable to extreme weather and high CO2 emissions, which can weaken household and corporate finances, repayment capacity, savings, and investment.
- Income statement impacts identified:
  - Net interest income: Potentially lower if clients’ investment capacity declines.
  - Allowances for insolvency risk: Likely higher due to deteriorated borrower solvency and reduced collateral values when climate risks materialize.
- Capital effects: Slight potential reduction in capital adequacy ratios from higher provisions and lower net income/returns.
- Scenario analysis outcome: Internal assessments indicate limited impact on the lending portfolio from both transition and physical risks.
- Risk management and mitigation:
  - Action plans and engagement to support client transition (NZBA commitment).
  - Portfolio rebalancing toward less GHG‑intensive clients and sectors.
  - Financing opportunities tied to adaptation and the energy transition, leveraging growing sustainable finance demand.
- Net interest income outlook: No negative impact expected in the short-to-medium term due to portfolio flexibility, client transition support, and diversification into sustainable projects.
- Provisions methodology: Downside scenarios incorporate structural reform shortfalls and macro dynamics (e.g., higher production and commodity costs) that depress productivity and GDP, reflecting exacerbated climate risk pathways.
- Scenario weightings used for provisioning (Spain and Portugal): Baseline 60%, Upside 20%, Downside 20% for 2022, 2023, and 2024.

nodes.title: Risk management and monitoring
nodes.heading: 1.4 Risk management and monitoring
nodes.start_phrase: The physical and transition risks associated with climate change are considered additional factors that have an impact on the previously defined risk categories, and their identification, measurement, management and monitoring are completely integrated into the Entity's risk management framework.
nodes.summary:
- The Entity fully integrates climate-related physical and transition risks into its overarching risk management framework, treating them as factors that influence existing risk categories and embedding them into governance processes in line with regulations and supervisory trends.
- Climate risk is incorporated across risk planning, corporate strategy, the risk catalogue, the risk appetite framework (RAF), risk assessment, and formalized through risk policies, frameworks, and processes.
- Climate risk metrics are embedded in monitoring and reporting circuits, with key indicators included at various RAF levels.
- Ongoing monitoring covers: concentration of the corporate portfolio in carbon-intensive sectors; financed emissions (with dedicated CO2 financed emissions methodology); decarbonization metrics aligned to NZBA targets; and mobilisation of sustainable finance.
- Additional regular monitoring includes exposures subject to transition risk by intensive sector; mortgage portfolio energy efficiency; exposures in the banking book to the top 20 global carbon‑intensive firms; and exposures subject to physical risk (note: physical risk exposure figures were corrected on October 31, 2024).

nodes.title: Integration of climate change in the management systems
nodes.heading: 1.4.1 Integration of climate change in the management systems
nodes.start_phrase: The physical and transition risks associated with climate change are considered additional factors that have an impact on the previously defined risk categories, and their identification, measurement, management and monitoring are completely integrated into the Entity's risk management framework.
nodes.summary:
- Climate change risks (physical and transition) are fully integrated into the Entity’s risk management framework, governance processes, policies, and strategic planning, including the risk catalogue, risk appetite framework, and risk assessments.
- Climate risk metrics are embedded in monitoring and reporting, with key indicators included in the risk appetite framework.
- Ongoing monitoring covers: portfolio concentration in carbon‑intensive corporate sectors; financed emissions; decarbonisation metrics aligned with NZBA targets; and mobilisation of sustainable finance.
- Additional tracked aspects include: exposures to transition risk by intensive sector; energy efficiency of the mortgage portfolio; banking book exposures to the top 20 global carbon‑intensive firms; and exposures subject to physical risk (with a correction noted on October 31, 2024).

nodes.title: Climate risk metrics
nodes.heading: 1.4.2 Climate risk metrics
nodes.start_phrase: Climate change metrics are included in the monitoring and reporting circuits, where key indicators have been included in the various levels of the risk appetite framework.
nodes.summary: The excerpt explains that the Entity fully embeds climate-related physical and transition risks into its enterprise risk management framework, governance, and strategic processes. Climate risk is integrated into risk planning, the risk catalogue, the risk appetite framework, and risk assessment, and is reflected in policies and processes. Climate risk metrics are part of regular monitoring and reporting, with key indicators set within the risk appetite. The Entity tracks portfolio concentration in carbon‑intensive sectors, financed emissions (per the “Calculation of CO2 emissions financed” section), progress against NZBA decarbonisation targets, and mobilisation of sustainable finance. Ongoing monitoring also covers exposures to transition risk by intensive sector, energy efficiency of the mortgage portfolio, exposures in the banking book to the top 20 carbon‑intensive firms, and exposures subject to physical risk (the latter corrected on October 31, 2024).
