  - Scope 3 category breakdowns: 3.1 Purchased goods and services (OPEX), 3.2 Capital goods (CAPEX), 3.3 Fuel- and energy-related activities (upstream and transmission/distribution), and 3.6 Business travel (air, rail, cars, hotels).

nodes.title: Reduction of CO Emissions2
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3 Reduction of CO Emissions2
nodes.start_phrase: With the aim of helping to reduce the Group's Carbon Footprint emissions, several initiatives have been implemented at the Group level.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Group-wide initiatives to reduce the carbon footprint, especially Scope 2 emissions, through the Environmental Management Plan’s seventh line of action on energy efficiency.
- Building and branch efficiency measures: LED lighting replacements, more efficient HVAC units, motion sensors and automatic light-off systems, timed switches, and upgraded computer equipment.
- Data centers: Two Data Processing Centres hold LEED certifications (one silver, one gold).
- Renewable electricity strategy: 100% of electricity consumption sourced from certified renewables, secured via PPAs (113.88 GWh/year, ~52% of total) and Guarantees of Origin (218.05 GWh/year).
- Fuel switch: In 2024, four diesel tanks were removed from branches by replacing existing air-conditioning equipment with heat pumps.
- Energy consumption results: 2024 Group energy use decreased 27.87% versus 2023 (-31.86% for CaixaBank, S.A.), driven by efficiency measures, merger synergies, and compliance with Spain’s Royal Decree-Law 14/2022 on energy saving.
- Monitoring and analytics: A centralized energy analytics platform aggregates data from building controls and meters to prioritize investments and implement best practices (optimized lighting/HVAC schedules, temperature setpoints, and equipment operation).
- Operational coverage and scale: 2,865 branches monitored; 1,093 branches remotely managed; 42 buildings monitored and/or remotely managed.
- Scope and applicability: Measures apply to Group companies covered by the Environmental Management Plan, representing 99.4% of CaixaBank Group employees.
- Headline metric: 100% of electricity consumed in 2024 was from certified renewable sources.

nodes.title: Promotion of energy efficiency.
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.1 1. Promotion of energy efficiency.
nodes.start_phrase: The promotion of energy efficiency is the seventh line of action in the Environmental Management Plan.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Group-wide initiatives to reduce the carbon footprint, especially Scope 2 emissions, through energy efficiency (line 7 of the Environmental Management Plan). The Plan covers Group companies representing 99.4% of employees.
- Energy efficiency in buildings/branches: LED retrofits, higher-efficiency HVAC replacements, motion sensors and automatic light-off systems, time-regulated switches, and upgraded computer equipment. In 2024, four diesel tanks were removed and replaced by heat pump systems.
- Data centers: Two Data Processing Centres hold LEED certifications (one Silver, one Gold).
- Renewable electricity strategy: 100% of electricity consumption in 2024 from certified renewable sources, secured via:
  - PPAs totaling 113.88 GWh/year (about 52% of total purchase).
  - Guarantees of Origin (GdO) totaling 218.05 GWh/year, certifying 100% of electricity purchased.
- Monitoring and analytics: An energy analytics platform aggregates consumption data from offices and buildings (via control/monitoring software and meter records) to prioritize investments and apply best practices—optimized lighting and HVAC schedules, temperature setpoints, and equipment operation.
- 2024 results: Group energy consumption fell 27.87% versus 2023 (-31.86% at CaixaBank, S.A.), driven by savings measures, merger synergies, and compliance with Spain’s Royal Decree-Law 14/2022, alongside climate and lighting factors.
- Operational reach of monitoring: 2,865 branches monitored, 1,093 branches remotely managed, and 42 buildings monitored and/or remotely managed.
- Overall: 100% renewable electricity consumption achieved in 2024.

nodes.title: Consumption and mix of energy sources

nodes.title: Boost in sustainable mobility
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.2 2. Boost in sustainable mobility
nodes.start_phrase: This corresponds to the fifth action line of the Environmental Management Plan.
nodes.summary: The document outlines CaixaBank’s “Boost in sustainable mobility” initiative, a key pillar of its Environmental Management Plan. It reports the 2023 creation of a cross-functional Sustainable Mobility Group to reduce emissions from corporate travel and describes a 360-degree Sustainable Mobility Plan that addresses internal corporate travel and external mobility by employees, customers, and suppliers. Implemented measures include expanding remote work and digital customer interactions to cut journeys; installing EV charging points and bicycle parking at corporate sites; downsizing the vehicle fleet and shifting to hybrids; using electric scooters for last‑mile deliveries; embedding environmental criteria in events and business trips; and conducting 2024 employee awareness campaigns on travel-related emissions. The plan’s scope targets four stakeholder groups: Company (embed policy and governance for fleet, travel, and events), Employees (enable low-impact commuting and reduce travel needs), Suppliers (cut pollution-related emissions and drive decarbonization), and Customers (offer sustainable mobility solutions, notably in electromobility).

nodes.title: Environmentalisation of procurement and contracts
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.3 3. Environmentalisation of procurement and contracts
nodes.start_phrase: By incorporating environmental criteria into the purchase of products and contracting of services, we extend our commitment to the suppliers and encourage them to adopt measures that minimise their activities' environmental impact.
nodes.summary:
- Embedding environmental criteria in procurement and service contracts to drive supplier adoption of practices that reduce environmental impact.
- 2024 enhancements to the Environmental Procurement Plan: creation of new green procurement/contracting sheets and inclusion of environmental compliance checks in supplier audits.
- Introduction of a mandatory Carbon Footprint questionnaire for key suppliers to quantify purchasing/contracting impacts and inform targets to reduce indirect (Scope 3) emissions.
- Waste and circular economy commitments aimed at cutting Scope 3 emissions, including:
  - Selective waste collection and recycling across facilities.
  - Authorized waste management in corporate buildings; cafeterias free of single-use plastics.
  - Branch network use of municipal selective collection for non-hazardous waste; authorized management of hazardous waste (bulbs, cooling gases, e-waste, toner).
  - Staff awareness campaigns to reduce waste generation.
  - Collection and recycling of obsolete cards; 100% of cards sold made from recycled PVC and biodegradable material.
  - ReUtilízame program facilitating donation of surplus materials to NGOs (2024: 66,597 items donated, 52 companies participating, 292 NGOs benefited).

nodes.title: Waste and commitment to the circular economy
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.4 Waste and commitment to the circular economy
nodes.start_phrase: CaixaBank considers good waste management to be essential, as well as the transition from linear consumption practices to circular consumption, with the aim of minimising its Scope 3 emissions in the Carbon Footprint.
nodes.summary:
- Environmentalisation of procurement and contracts: CaixaBank embeds environmental criteria into purchasing and service contracts to drive supplier environmental performance. In 2024 it expanded the Environmental Procurement Plan with new green procurement/contracting sheets and began integrating compliance checks into supplier audits. A mandatory Carbon Footprint questionnaire for key suppliers was introduced to improve data on indirect (Scope 3) impacts and inform emission-reduction targets.

- Waste and circular economy commitments: To cut Scope 3 emissions, the bank advances selective waste collection and recycling, uses authorised waste managers at corporate buildings, and operates cafeterias without single-use plastics. Across branches, non-hazardous waste uses municipal selective collection; hazardous waste (bulbs, cooling gases, e-waste, toner) is handled by authorised managers. Ongoing staff awareness campaigns, collection of obsolete cards for recycling, and a shift to 100% recycled PVC and biodegradable materials for sold cards are highlighted. The ReUtilízame program facilitates donations of surplus materials to NGOs (open to customers); in 2024, 66,597 items were donated by 52 companies, benefiting 292 NGOs. Waste data feed into CaixaBank S.A.’s carbon footprint, with reductions from 2021 to 2024: toner cartridges from 42 t to 28 t and IT support waste from 1,262 t to 414 t.

nodes.title: Paper
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.5 Paper
nodes.start_phrase: In recent years, several initiatives at Group level have been implemented to reduce paper consumption1:

- Paper management:
  - Group-wide digitisation enables 100% digital signatures; ATMs support envelope-free deposits and screen-only receipts; invoicing is fully electronic.

nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.3.6 Water

nodes.title: Offsetting CO2 emissions
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.1.4 Offsetting CO2 emissions
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the Environmental Management Plan, the CaixaBank Group has undertaken to neutralise the carbon footprint (Carbon Neutral) of its own activity for Scope 1, 2 and for category 3.6 corporate travel of Scope 3.
nodes.summary:
- Commitment and scope: CaixaBank targets carbon neutrality for Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 category 3.6 (corporate travel), prioritizing emission reductions first and offsetting only the residual.
- Offsetting approach in 2024: Shift to 100% GHG removal projects (no reduction projects), with 19,736 tCO2e offset at a cost of €447,168. Carbon credits are used only for neutralization and are not counted toward the reported footprint or reduction targets; no credits are banked for future years nor contracted beyond the current year.
- Offset project mix and standards: 
  - 50% Spain (Ourense, Galicia) reforestation under MITECO, Vintage 2023.
  - 40% Uruguay (Montes del Este) forest project under VCS, Vintage 2019.
  - 10% Mexico (Quintana Roo) forest project under CAR, Vintage 2022+.
  - 50% of credits within the EU; no corresponding adjustments under Paris Agreement Article 6.
- Year-on-year view: 2024 removals 100% vs. 75% in 2023; standards split in 2024—MITECO 50%, VCS 40%, CAR 10%.
- Own absorption projects: Two CaixaBank-led reforestations (Montserrat, Barcelona; Ejulve, Teruel) validated by MITECO; permanence risk managed via a guarantee fund. These nature-based projects provide environmental co-benefits and play a primarily symbolic role in demonstrating commitment.
- Value chain engagement: Not directly involved in removal/storage with value-chain agents; 2024 supplier questionnaire added questions on carbon footprint compensation efforts.
- Environmental Management Plan 2025–2027: Continues focus on impact mitigation, measurement, and reduction via six action lines:
  1) Climate change: 100% renewable energy (supplier + PPAs) and internal carbon pricing.
  2) Sustainable procurement: Supplier engagement on footprints and targets; maintain/extend the Environmental Plan for Procurement and Contracts.
  3) Circular economy: Donation program (ReÚtilizame) and reuse of plastic from obsolete bank cards.
  4) Sustainable mobility: Reduce corporate fleet; expand EV charging and carsharing; awareness to cut travel emissions.
  5) Efficiency: HVAC replacement; branch automation, LED, efficient climate control, operational best practices; digitization to reduce paper/toner/cards; review documentary management.
  6) Certifications: Extend ISO 14001 scope and increase number of events certified as sustainable.

nodes.title: Environmental Management Plan 2025-2027
nodes.heading: 1.6.5.2 Environmental Management Plan 2025-2027
nodes.start_phrase: This new Environmental Management Plan maintains the main lines of action followed by the previous plan, focusing on mitigating the environmental impact of the Group's activities, measuring its impact through the calculation of the carbon footprint, and prioritising its reduction through initiatives related to efficiency, the circular economy, engagement with the value chain, sustainable mobility, and the implementation of new certifications.
nodes.summary:
- CaixaBank runs two in-house CO2 absorption (reforestation) projects in Montserrat (Barcelona) and Ejulve (Teruel), which it has promoted, financed, and managed.
- Both projects are registered and validated by Spain’s MITECO; permanence risk is managed via a guarantee fund, and absorption is calculated per MITECO Climate Change Office methodology.
- The forests function as natural carbon sinks and deliver co-benefits (soil protection, erosion and landslide prevention, biodiversity), serving as nature-based solutions; their carbon impact is modest and primarily symbolic of CaixaBank’s local environmental commitment.
- CaixaBank is not currently involved in GHG removal/storage projects with value-chain partners, but in 2024 added supplier questionnaire items on carbon footprint compensation to identify supplier efforts.
- The Environmental Management Plan 2025–2027 continues the prior strategy: measure and reduce the operational carbon footprint and environmental impacts through efficiency, circular economy, value-chain engagement, sustainable mobility, and certifications.
- Six action lines and key initiatives:
  1) Climate change: 100% renewable energy (including PPA) and internal carbon pricing.
  2) Greener procurement/contracts: supplier engagement on carbon footprint and targets; extend the Environmental Plan for Procurement and Contracts.
  3) Circular economy: ReÚtilizame donation program (IT, furniture); reuse plastic from obsolete bank cards.
  4) Sustainable mobility: smaller corporate fleet; more EV charging and carsharing; travel-emissions awareness.
  5) Efficiency: replace HVAC; branch automation, LEDs, efficient climate control, operational best practices; digitisation to cut paper/toner/cards; review documentary management.
  6) Certifications: extend ISO 14001 scope and sustainable events.
- Emissions-reduction approach is based on internal criteria tailored to CaixaBank’s operations rather than external climate scenarios; targets address impacts from the Double Materiality Study, focusing on reducing the internal and operational carbon footprint.
- Quantitative targets (baseline 2024) for CaixaBank and the Group:
  - Scope 1 reductions: by 2025/26/27/2030 = -9%/-12%/-16%/-22% (CaixaBank) and -4%/-6%/-7%/-10% (Group).
  - Scope 2 (market method): 0 tCO2 each year (reflecting 100% renewable electricity).
  - Scope 2 (location method) reductions: -5%/-8%/-10%/-15% (CaixaBank) and -4%/-6%/-7.5%/-11% (Group).
  - Scope 1+2 reductions (market method): -9%/-12%/-16%/-22% (CaixaBank) and -4%/-6%/-7%/-10% (Group).
  - Scope 1+2 reductions (location method): -6%/-9%/-11%/-16% (CaixaBank) and -4%/-6%/-7.5%/-11% (Group).
  - Offsetting: 100% of Scopes 1, 2, and corporate travel (Scope 3.6) annually.
  - Renewable electricity consumption: 100% annually.
  - Electricity savings: -5%/-8%/-10%/-15% (CaixaBank) and -4%/-6%/-7.5%/-11% (Group).
- Scope 1 and 2 targets cover 100% of the operational footprint perimeter; the Sustainability Committee monitors these targets.

structure.title: Green taxonomy
structure.heading: Green taxonomy
structure.start_phrase: In 2020, the European Parliament and the EU Council adopted Regulation (EU) 2020/852, hereinafter the Taxonomy Regulation , which establishes uniform and common criteria in the European Union to determine if an economic activity can be considered environmentally sustainable.
structure.summary:
- Introduces the EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852 and its purpose: harmonized criteria to assess whether economic activities are environmentally sustainable.
- Lists the six environmental objectives: climate change mitigation and adaptation, sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources, transition to a circular economy, pollution prevention and control, and protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems. Notes the 2023 extension of activities and remaining objectives.
- Explains alignment requirements: activities must meet technical screening criteria, Do No Significant Harm (DNSH), and minimum social safeguards.
- Describes transparency and disclosure obligations under Article 8: firms subject to NFRD must report eligibility and alignment; financial companies had a one‑year deferral. With CSRD from 2025, scope expands to large unlisted, listed SMEs, and certain non‑EU entities. Notes EC FAQs published in Dec 2023 for KPI guidance.
- Outlines phased disclosure timeline (2021–2025): eligibility and alignment for climate objectives first, then other objectives; KPIs include Green Asset Ratio (GAR) and Green Investment Ratio (GIR); separate disclosures for nuclear and gas.
- Defines eligibility vs alignment and the key ratios:
  - Eligibility ratio: share of assets/investments fitting Taxonomy activity descriptions.
  - GAR (banking and insurance assets) and GIR (asset management, pension plans, EPSV): share aligned with Taxonomy among “assets/investments covered.”
- Details calculation methodologies and exclusions:
  - Banking Group (prudential perimeter CRR/CRD IV): denominator excludes sovereigns/supranationals/central banks and trading book; numerator further excludes non‑NFRD companies, derivatives (hedging), cash/interbank, and certain other assets. Alignment requires meeting technical criteria, DNSH, and minimum safeguards.
  - Insurance Group and Pension Plans/EPSV: analogous coverage, exclusions, and alignment tests.
  - Mandatory reporting is based primarily on counterparties’ own KPIs (turnover and CapEx).
- Discloses exposure reporting to nuclear energy and fossil gas per Delegated Regulations (EU) 2022/1214, 2021/2139, and 2021/2178.
- Notes data sources, limitations, and interpretation:
  - Reliance on counterparties’ disclosures; supplementary ESG data via MSCI; conservative approach where data is missing (treated as not eligible/aligned).
  - Complexity and interpretive uncertainty around technical criteria, DNSH, and minimum safeguards; significant use of professional judgment.
  - GAR’s representativeness is affected by balance sheet composition, especially exposures to non‑NFRD entities (e.g., SMEs, non‑EU), which depress the ratio.
- Clarifies reporting scope and valuation:
  - Taxonomy prepared on a prudential basis; differences vs accounting consolidation (e.g., equity method for certain entities under prudential rules).
  - Financial assets at amortized cost are valued at gross carrying amount for Taxonomy templates.
- Presents 2024 results and insights:
  - Banking Group: GAR 3.05% (turnover KPI) and 3.93% (CapEx KPI). Eligibility ratios are higher than alignment due to exclusions and data gaps. Methodology update increased 2024 GAR versus 2023 by revising DNSH assessment for retail mortgages using the bank’s Pillar 3 physical risk methodology; households are not subject to minimum social safeguards. Aligned mortgage portfolio reached €7,471m at 31 Dec 2024; on a comparable basis, 2023 GAR would have been 2.30% instead of 1.05%. Expanded collection of Energy Efficiency Certificates and inclusion of certain exposures where counterparties fall under Accounting Directive Articles 19a/29a.
  - Insurance business (VidaCaixa): GAR 3.33% (turnover) and 4.94% (CapEx). Increase driven by classifying certain green bonds as aligned (use‑of‑proceeds consistent with Taxonomy) and greater availability of alignment data for NFRD financials; denominator mix affected by incorporating third‑party fund manager data.
  - Pension Plans and EPSV: GIR 2.48% (turnover) and 3.46% (CapEx).
- Provides additional conglomerate KPIs (banking + insurance): weighted average KPI 3.10% (turnover) and 4.12% (CapEx), based on ordinary income weights.
- Concludes with outlook: ratios expected to rise as remaining objectives are included, counterparty data availability improves, and regulatory clarity increases; the Group will enhance disclosures on counterparties’ alignment as new requirements become applicable.

structure.start_phrase:
Employees are a key stakeholder group for CaixaBank, which is why the emphasis in the 2022-2024 Strategic Plan is on people as a fundamental driver, aiming to 
address the challenge of:
structure.summary:
- Strategic people agenda and 2022-2024 results:

- Workforce profile and evolution:
  - Total staff 46,014 (+2.6% YoY): Spain 41,304; Portugal 4,426; Others 284.
  - Gender split: 56.1% women, 43.9% men; average age 46.8; average tenure 18.7 years.
  - New hires 2,116; headcount growth driven by technical roles and network staffing.

- 2025-2027 Strategic Plan (people priorities):
  - Ambition to be the best company to work for.
  - Lines of action: attract/retain top talent (employer brand, 360° engagement model, wellbeing), accelerate transformation of existing talent (skills planning, AI, agility, project management, upskilling/reskilling), strengthen a culture of proximity, agility and collaboration under the AHEAD leadership model.
  - Generational balance: ~3,000 young hires planned; target under-35s at 11.4% by 2027.

- Diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI):
  - Comprehensive framework via the Equality Plan and Wengage programme (gender, generational, functional/disability, LGTBI, cultural diversity), with governance through internal Diversity Committee and External Advisory Committee.
  - Gender: promotion of female leadership (Impulsa Plan, mentoring), unbiased recruitment, pay equity analysis; recognitions include Bloomberg GEI and multiple DEI awards/certifications.
  - Pay equity: adjusted gender pay gap 1.0% Group (0.9% Spain; 2.0% Portugal); gross pay gap down to 14% overall; continued actions to narrow gaps by 2027.
  - Functional diversity: formal inclusion policy, workplace adaptations, targeted hiring partnerships; employees with disabilities up to 650 (1.4%).
  - LGTBI and cultural diversity: guidance, awareness campaigns, new cultural diversity action plan.

- Talent development and training:
  - Development by Skills model: unified skills architecture, Skills Review and AHEAD Review assessments, tailored upskilling/reskilling plans; PeopleSkills platform launched to manage skills and recommend training.
  - Leadership development under AHEAD model with 360° reviews and targeted programmes; coaching and mentoring embedded.
  - Training scale: 2.99 million hours; €15.4m invested; 100% of staff trained; 92.5% online; 65.9 hours/employee; satisfaction 4.1/5.
  - Regulatory certifications (LCCI, IDD, MiFID II) and a robust Sustainability Training Plan.

- Working conditions, labour rights and collective bargaining:
  - Strong compliance with labour standards; constructive social dialogue.
  - New 2024–2026 sector agreement: cumulative 11% wage table increase (5%/3%/3%), €1,000 lump-sum, extra personal day, removal of entry level XIV.
  - Coverage: 99.8% under collective bargaining; 97.6% represented by worker representatives.
  - Job stability: 99.6% permanent contracts; goal to maintain ~100%.
  - Human rights commitments (no forced/child labour; non-discrimination; accessible reporting channels).

- Compensation and benefits:
  - Revised General Remuneration Policy (2024): meritocratic, competitive, non-discriminatory, aligned with long-term value and ESG risk mitigation.
  - Variable pay integrates ESG metrics for all staff (customer quality NPS mix; sustainable finance mobilisation), with disclosed targets and achievements.
  - Extensive benefits: pension plan contributions (€179m), insurance (€21m), enhanced employee loans, flexible remuneration (Compensa+), entry-level pay above local minimums (Spain 1.2x; Portugal 1.5x); total compensation ratio (highest paid vs median) of 62.

  - Healthy Organisation strategy with AENOR certification and TOP Wellbeing recognition.
  - Broad wellbeing initiatives: Wellbeing Week, expanded psychological support, emotional wellbeing programmes.

- Employee engagement and dialogue:

structure.title: S3-Communities affected
structure.heading: S3-Communities affected
structure.start_phrase:
Social commitment is one of CaixaBank's main assets 
and differential values, which has been integrated into 
its activity, but goes beyond it, through solutions 
that meet the needs of people and social projects 
that improve their wellbeing.
structure.summary:
- Theme and commitment: CaixaBank embeds social action into its core activity to drive positive change, prioritising a fair, inclusive society. It focuses on amplifying “la Caixa” Foundation programmes, building partnerships, delivering tailored social banking for vulnerable groups, addressing urgent social challenges, and fostering solidarity through extensive volunteering.

- Policy and governance framework: Actions are guided by the Principles of Action on Sustainability (integral, responsible, and sustainable action; unrivalled service; economic efficiency; long-term vision; innovation), complemented by the Sustainability Master Plan, Code of Ethics, and Human Rights Principles. The approach aligns with international standards and the UN SDGs.

- Community engagement: Ongoing, structured dialogue with “la Caixa” Foundation, major NGOs (e.g., Red Cross, ONCE), territorial social action managers, and social entities via regular meetings and focus groups informs priorities. Effectiveness is reviewed with partners and through monthly internal monitoring of community investments.

- 2024 scale and focus: €7.2M provided directly by CaixaBank and €75.2M channelled from “la Caixa” Foundation and customers. Interventions tackled illness/disability, poverty, labour integration, multiculturalism and social exclusion, senior care, education, basic needs, and environment. CaixaBank was named Global Finance’s “World’s Best Bank for its support of Society 2024.”

- Key programmes with “la Caixa” Foundation:
  - Decentralised Social Action: ~€25M directed through the branch network to thousands of local projects and entities, heavily supporting illness/disability, multiculturalism/exclusion, poverty, seniors, and employment.
  - Solidarity formulas: 62 agreements mobilising €0.52M from companies and individuals to complement local projects.
  - “Ningún Hogar Sin Alimentos”: €1.7M raised (including €1.0M from the Foundation), providing 1,548 tonnes of food to 54 food banks.

- Partnerships with regional foundations:
  - Social calls: €1.03M supporting 228 projects (vulnerable groups, seniors, quality of life).
  - Environmental call with Fundación Montemadrid: €0.12M for 14 biodiversity/circular economy projects.
  - Sociocultural initiatives with 11 territorial foundations: €1.62M for courses, workshops, and cultural/charitable actions.

- Other collaborations and own programmes:
  - Youth congresses (Fundación Lo Que De Verdad Importa and Relife): 13,895 attendees on values and addiction prevention.
  - Tree of Dreams: 34,136 beneficiaries (including a pilot for isolated seniors); customer and employee gift sponsorships.
  - Full of Life (seniors): €0.16M for workshops in health, personal development, and digital skills across 301 towns.
  - Land of Opportunities (rural depopulation): €0.63M; 1,966 entrepreneurs supported and 168 winning projects to create jobs and retain population.
  - ReUtilízame (circular economy): 66,597 donated items from 52 companies to 292 social entities.

- Support to the third social sector:
  - Donation platform (branches and digital): €48.64M raised for 2,783 causes and 2,311 entities, including €22.8M for the Valencia flooding emergency and extensive volunteer mobilisation.

- Volunteering:
  - Open to employees, customers, and society; structured into strategic, local, and emergency actions, with a new Volunteering Campus for training.
  - 2024 outcomes: 20,201 volunteers, 29,935 activities, 433,514 beneficiaries, 2,509 collaborating entities.
  - Social Month: 16,580 volunteers, 2,749 activities; 37% of CaixaBank Group staff participated.
  - Activity mix: 68% accompaniment, 28% education, 2% environment, 1% digitalisation, 1% other.
  - “Everyone’s Project”: €756,000 donated to 150 projects nominated by employee volunteers.

- BPI (Portugal) social commitment with “la Caixa” Foundation:
  - Social programmes: BPI “la Caixa” Awards (€5.1M; 133 projects; 18,096 beneficiaries) across disability, inclusion, seniors, and childhood.
  - PROMOVE: €5.2M for 18 pilot and 11 R&D mobilising projects in inland regional development.
  - Decentralised social initiative (ISD): €1.9M; 330 projects; ~70,000 direct beneficiaries.
  - Research and health: €7.7M for 9 projects (neurodegenerative, oncological, cardiovascular, infectious diseases, enabling technologies).

structure.title: S4-Customers
structure.heading: S4-Customers
structure.start_phrase: CaixaBank works to increase customer satisfaction and enhance the customer experience by implementing various communication channels and experience measurement models.
structure.summary:
- Strategic focus on customers: CaixaBank prioritizes satisfaction, multi‑channel engagement, and experience measurement, with commitments to transparency, anti‑greenwashing, inclusion, entrepreneurship, financial education, and rigorous data protection. Double Materiality IROs highlight opportunities in new channels and education and risks in greenwashing and data loss. Client base: 20.3 million (18.5M Spain; 1.8M Portugal).
- Respect for human rights: Access to services, integrating social/environmental risks in decisions, avoiding financing tied to serious human rights violations, and safeguarding confidentiality and privacy, as set out in the Group’s Human Rights Principles.
- Customer experience model: “Listen–Understand–Act” with AI‑driven insights, continuous NPS tracking (relational, transactional, digital) linked to remuneration, and 2025–2027 goal to rank No. 1 in digital satisfaction. 2024 activity included >6M survey responses, 4M+ relational surveys, 37.6M transactional surveys, and real‑time “Close the Loop” remediation plus a Customer Service Improvement Plan (MAC). NPS and experience indicators improved across segments.
- Transparent and responsible marketing: Updated Corporate Commercial Communication Policy (Dec‑2024) mandates legality, clarity, balance, objectivity, and transparency; participation in Autocontrol pre‑clearance. Large volumes of campaigns reviewed with most approved or approved with modifications. Broad employee certification base (MiFID, LCCI, IDD).
- Responsible lending and clear contracts: Policies align with Bank of Spain circular on responsible lending; solvency assessment prioritizes repayment capacity and fair treatment. “Transparent contract” project uses plain language and digital‑first design; 42 key contracts updated to improve clarity, trust, and legal certainty.
- Product governance and greenwashing prevention: Corporate Product Governance Policy (Nov‑2024) and dual committees (Product Strategy; Transparency) oversee product lifecycle; 2024: 23 sessions, 266 products analyzed, 6 initially rejected. Automated ESG product classification (SFDR Articles 8/9, PAIs, Taxonomy) and robust controls (Sustainable Financing Guide, specialist teams, monthly reviews) to avoid greenwashing.
- Customer service and complaints: Omni‑channel Contact Center (phone, web, email, chat, social) with NPS monitoring (66.6% in 2024) and expanded branch phone service. Dedicated senior line handled 1.04M calls. Total interactions: 10.25M (+33.75% YoY). Independent Customer Service Office (SAC) manages complaints, reports to governance bodies; 2024 complaint volumes increased, with improved timeliness and a significant share resolved in favor of claimants; detailed breakdowns by product/channel.
- ESG client engagement: ESG advisory for corporates/institutions; acted as ESG Coordinator in sustainable syndicated lending; new regional sustainability team for Company Banking and structured client support through governance, diagnosis, materiality, and strategy phases.
- Financial inclusion, accessibility, and proximity: Omnichannel accessibility roadmap aligned to EU Accessibility Act, with accessible design principles and specific solutions (Braille card, accessible POS, sign‑language pilot). High accessibility in branches (Spain 89%; Portugal 75%) and 100% accessible ATMs with visual, acoustic, tactile, and senior‑friendly features. Inclusive app/website (WCAG‑aligned, ILUNION‑audited). Largest physical network and commitment to rural presence: 3,570 branches in Spain, 1,403 rural branches, 28 mobile branches serving 1,294 towns (644k people; 70% seniors).
- Solutions for vulnerable groups: MicroBank drives inclusion via microcredits for families (low‑income thresholds), social‑impact loans, and programs like Proyecto Confianza. Protocols to prevent financial abuse of people with disabilities/elderly; basic payment accounts with fee exemptions for vulnerable customers (362,728). Senior support includes specialized advisors/lines, adapted ATMs, dedicated products (e.g., MyBox Senior), in‑person training, and AENOR certification as an organization committed to seniors.
- Equal treatment and non‑discrimination: Plan under Law 15/2022 identifies priority vulnerable groups and adds protocols for detection/reporting of abuse (cases referred to Prosecutor’s Office), autonomy‑preserving procedures for victims, and accessibility pilots (e.g., sign‑language).
- Support for social entities and social housing: Specific products for third‑sector organizations (19,416 accounts) and NGO affinity cards; roadmap to expand offerings. Social housing policy combines early, specialized care (Mortgage Customer Service) and participation in public programs (Government’s Social Housing Fund). 2024: 9,536 social‑rent contracts with adapted rents; ongoing “Impulsa” social support.
- Financial education and health: Comprehensive literacy plan for multiple audiences (shareholders, youth, vulnerable adults, people with intellectual disabilities, seniors, entrepreneurs), delivered via conferences, workshops, in‑branch sessions, and digital content (webinars, podcasts, videos). Notable initiatives include Shareholder Aula, youth programs via imagin and in schools, MicroBank Academy with Google, and sector‑specific training (e.g., catering).
- Employability and entrepreneurship: MicroBank financing supports entrepreneurs, self‑employed, social enterprises, agro generational renewal, and education (Skills & Education loans for students and schools with EIF). 2024 outcomes include businesses created, jobs supported, and sizable financing volumes; broad partner network of public/private entities and European institutions (EIB, EIF, CEB). Cumulative jobs since 2022 exceed targets; new 2025–2027 goal to improve employability for 150,000 people. CaixaBank Dualiza advances vocational training through grants, events, teacher/student programs, and research, benefiting tens of thousands.
- Privacy and personal data protection: Board‑led governance, Corporate Privacy Policy (updated 2024) covering ethical data/AI use, and two corporate committees (Privacy; PIA). Transparent client communications (policy updated semi‑annually, multiple rights channels, in‑app controls), structured consent capture, and rigorous records/DPIA methodology aligned with AEPD guidance. Centralized breach management with monthly oversight, integration with HR/disciplinary processes, and continuous training/awareness tied to variable pay. Ongoing monitoring of regulatory changes and reinforced cybersecurity to minimize data‑related risks.

structure.title: G-Governance

- Emphasis on good corporate governance as a foundation for strategy, daily decision-making, and stakeholder relationships, grounded in values of integrity, respect, honesty, transparency, and professional excellence.
- Strong compliance framework: adherence to strict national and international regulations translated into internal policies with monitoring of operational effectiveness and compliance.
- People-centric business conduct: transparency with customers, shareholders, and investors; robust AML/CFT measures; active prevention of corruption and bribery; no contracting of direct lobbying or interest representation services; strict personal data protection; extension of governance standards across the value chain.
- Speak-up culture: ensuring an open, safe environment for employees to raise concerns to enable early detection of conduct and behavioral breaches.
- High priority on combating bribery, corruption, and financial crime; AML/CFT recognized as a material issue due to sector risks.
- Commitment to transparency regarding any lobbying activities, despite their limited scope.
- Supplier stewardship: supporting suppliers to improve sustainability and align with CaixaBank’s objectives and values; enhanced ESG compliance through supplier audits.
- Process to identify and assess material impacts, risks, and opportunities in business conduct: annual Risk Assessment covering conduct and compliance risks in the corporate risk catalogue; integration into a Double Materiality Study alongside stakeholder expectations, market practices, the Code of Ethics, and market trends.
- Key risks identified: non-adaptation or non-compliance with ESG regulations; inadequate risk management (including conflicts of interest and alignment with risk appetite), potentially leading to penalties or loss of trust; non-compliance with AML/CFT, corruption, and bribery requirements; lack of transparency in relations with public institutions.
- Key impacts/opportunities identified: promotion of ethical culture with customers, suppliers, and other stakeholders; contribution to public finances through tax payments; increased supplier ESG compliance resulting from audits.
